en: The Legend of King Aśoka, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Fǎqīn of Parthia during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Account of the Original Gift of the Land. The Account of the Original Gift of the Land.
Homage to the All-Knowing Bhagavān.
Residing at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha,
at that time the World-Honored One’s mealtime had arrived.
Having put on his robes and taken up his alms bowl, surrounded by the bhikṣus before and behind him,
he proceeded toward Rājagṛha to beg for food in succession.
The commentator says:
Immovable like a mountain of gold, Dignified and composed like a king of elephants,
With limbs as perfect as the full moon,
The Bhikṣu-saṃgha surrounded him as he proceeded toward the great city of Rājagṛha, His deportment exceedingly orderly and serene.
When he finally reached the city and stepped upon the threshold of the gate,
the great earth immediately shook in six ways.
The narrator said:
The ocean adorns the earth, and the mountain city does likewise;
when the Muni treads upon its threshold, all things surge and subside.
Thus, as he enters the city, men and women give rise to pure faith.
The entire city was transformed; like waves stirred by the wind, all things emitted harmonious and elegant sounds—never before seen in this world.
As the Buddha entered the city, the mounds and ruins were all leveled and made smooth.
There shall be no sand, gravel, thorns, or filth; all shall sink into the earth.
The blind shall see, the deaf shall hear, the mute shall speak, and the lame shall stand up.
The mad shall regain their minds, the impoverished shall obtain wealth, and the sick shall be healed—there shall be every form of joy.
Without being struck, the precious vessels resounded of their own accord, emitting various sounds.
The Buddha’s light shone everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns;
its brilliance was so penetrating that both the interior and exterior were entirely golden. The radiance he emitted eclipsed the sun and the moon.
Illuminating sentient beings, it brings cooling relief to their parching heat;
just as when sandalwood is applied to a feverish ailment, there is nothing that is not extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One was with Ānanda in the street.
As he was walking along, he saw two young boys:
one named Deśeṣa, a son of a noble family,
and the other named Anuśeṣa, a son of a secondary noble family.
He played with the earth, building a city out of it;
within the city, he further constructed houses and storehouses,
and placed flour made of earth inside the storehouses.
These two children saw the Buddha’s body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
He emitted golden light that illuminated both the interior and exterior of the city,
turning everything golden and leaving nothing unpenetrated by its brilliance.
Having seen this, he was filled with joy.
Devasena then took a handful of soil from the granary, which was called "flour," and offered it to the World-Honored One.
While standing by his side, Anabhibhū joined his palms in sympathetic rejoicing.
At that time, Deśeṇa spoke this verse in praise:
"The Greatly Compassionate One, the Teacherless Awakened One, With a body radiant with a perfect halo—
Though my face was flushed with shame, I gave rise to reverent faith And offered earth to the Tathāgata."
I prostrate to the World-Honored One, who has already severed birth and death.
At that time, the youth Guṇavara,
having finished offering the earth, made this aspiration:
"May I, in the future, cover heaven and earth.
He then spoke a verse in offering.
The speaker said:
The Buddha, knowing that child’s mind and his aspiration for a pure vow,
[perceived] that because of this supreme field of merit, he would certainly obtain a great fruit;
the Greatly Compassionate Savior of the World immediately accepted that land.
Causing his heart to rejoice, he thus plants the causal conditions for the kingly enterprise.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately smiled.
Ānanda knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
the Buddha does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what conditions has he manifested this smile?
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
"He who has severed sorrow and pride is the most supreme in the world.
It is never without cause or condition that his teeth appear as white as conch shells or lotus roots."
Like the sound of thunder emerging from clouds, you who possess the eye-mark of a bull king, pray tell me of the reward for giving land and the matter of your smile.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: [as follows].
"It is so, Ānanda; it is so. The Buddha does not smile without cause.
Do you see these two children now?
"I have seen them, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said: "One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, this boy shall become a Cakravartin King who possesses one-fourth of its power.
In the city of Pāṭaliputra, he shall rule as a righteous king known as Aśoka."
"Divide my relics and construct eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas for the benefit of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a king named Aśoka."
His fame shall spread far and wide; his reliquaries shall be magnificently adorned and fill the entire Jambudvīpa, receiving the offerings of gods and humans.
By the cause of giving even a small amount of earth, he receives this great retribution.
Having spoken these verses,
the Buddha then gave this earth to Ānanda,
instructing him to smear it upon the ground where the Tathāgata would walk, and he spoke these words:
Ānanda, the prince of Bimbisāra was named Ajātaśatru;
the son of Ajātaśatru was named Udayanabhadra.
The son of Udraka Rāmaputra was named Munda;
the son of Munda was named Acelaka;
the son of Acelaka was named Saṃjaya.
The son of Śvapāka was named Dūraga;
Dūraga’s son was named Svāgata-maṇḍala;
Svāgata-maṇḍala’s son was named Prasenajit.
The son of Prasenajit was named Nanda.
The son of Nanda was King Bimbisāra.
In the city of Pāṭaliputra, the son of Bimbisāra was named Ajātaśatru.
In the kingdom of Campā, there was a brāhmaṇa who gave birth to a daughter of jewel-like beauty.
A physiognomist divined that she would surely become a queen and be the king’s favorite.
"You shall give birth to two precious sons:
one shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King ruling over a quarter of the world;
the other shall leave the household life and attain the state of an Arhat."
Upon hearing this, the brāhmaṇa was filled with extreme joy;
he then took the girl to the city of Puṣpapura and adorned her with various precious jewels and necklaces.
She was given in marriage to King Bimbisāra as his queen,
and the king immediately took her into his harem.
The consorts and ladies of the palace all conceived feelings of jealousy and thought to themselves:
"The King will surely hold us in contempt and treat us as lowly.
We must teach him a base craft that he will come to loathe.
They then instructed him until he became highly skilled in shaving hair and beards.
While the king was asleep, he had him shave his beard.
When the king woke from sleep, he said,
"Shave my beard for me."
He replied, "It has been shaved.
The king immediately looked at himself in a mirror;
knowing that his beard had been completely shaved, he spoke to him, saying:
"What wish do you desire to fulfill?
She replied, "I seek only to have union with the King.
The King said, "I am a Kṣatriya."
"Your body is lowly and base; how could there be a union?
The woman replied to the king, "I am not of low birth;
I am the daughter of a brāhmaṇa."
Originally, the Brahmin intended for me to become the king's wife;
however, the palace ladies, out of jealousy, taught me this lowly craft.
The king then said to her, "From this day forward, do not do such a thing."
She was then established as the first consort;
they lived together in mutual love and affection, and a son was born.
The mother said, "My anxieties and afflictions are now entirely removed."
He immediately gave him a name, Aśoka;
"Aśoka" means "Sorrowless" in the Jin language. Later, another son was born, named Viśoka.
Aśoka’s body was coarse and rough, so his father did not love or cherish him.
Bimbisāra also begot many sons by his various consorts.
He assembled all the physiognomists to examine the features of these sons.
Among them was a physiognomist named Piṅgalavatsājīva.
The king said to this physiognomist, "Divine among my sons which one shall become king.
The physiognomist replied, "Your Majesty, lead your sons toward the Golden Ground Garden (Suvarṇabhūmi-udyāna) and have them examined there."
The king and his sons arrived at the Kāñcanamālā Garden.
The mother commanded Aśoka, saying,
"Now that the king’s son has gone to the Kāñcanamālā Garden, you too may go there."
Aśoka said, "The King does not love me; why should I go there?
His mother replied again, "You must certainly go.
Aśoka said, "I shall go."
Afterward, he brought food to me and then took his leave and departed.
Upon leaving the city of Puṣpapura, he met the son of the prime minister, Rādha-gupta.
Rādha-gupta asked Aśoka:
"Where do you wish to go?
He replied, "The King has gathered his sons to visit the Golden Ground Garden; I now wish to go there as well."
At that time, Kūṭadanta mounted an old elephant and said to Aśoka, "You may mount this elephant.
Aśoka immediately mounted the elephant and proceeded toward the Golden Ground Garden (Suvarṇabhūmi-udyāna).
He immediately went to the garden and descended from the elephant;
he sat upon the ground beside his sons,
while the sons all ate various kinds of delicacies.
Aśoka ate boiled rice, served in earthenware vessels and mixed with curd; when thirsty, he drank water.
The king said to the physiognomist, "Preceptor, please examine my sons."
"After my death, who shall rightfully become king?
The physiognomist thought to himself, "Aśoka must surely be the one to become king.
I then replied to the king, "He is the one who ought to be king."
"The King will not spare me and will surely kill me.
He then replied to the King, "It is not appropriate to speak of his name;
rather, one may describe his physical appearance. Whoever possesses the foremost articles of attire and equipment shall be the King."
Each of the princes, individually,
mounted the foremost vehicle, sat upon the foremost seat,
ate the foremost food from the foremost vessel, and drank the foremost beverage.
Aśoka thought to himself, "I ought to become king.
Why is this? For the elephant is the foremost of vehicles."
The earth is the foremost seat;
non-glutinous rice is the foremost food;
and earthenware vessels are the foremost containers.
Curd is the foremost of flavors;
water is the foremost of beverages.
For this reason, I ought to be king.
Having finished the physiognomy,
the king led his sons back into the city.
The physiognomist spoke to the mother of Aśoka, saying:
"Aśoka will certainly become king.
His mother said to the physiognomist, "Do not speak of this again;
we must all hide ourselves far away as if protecting our very lives."
"Wait until Aśoka has succeeded to the royal throne, and then you may come forth.
King Bindusāra, because Takṣaśilā had rebelled and remained unsubmissive,
immediately dispatched Aśoka to go and subdue that kingdom.
He was accompanied only by the fourfold army and carried no swords or staves.
At that time, Aśoka received his orders and immediately departed from the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Those around him remarked, "There are no swords or staves."
"How can one engage in battle with an enemy?
Aśoka replied, "I possess the power of merit and am destined to be a king;
whatever weapons, such as swords and staves, I require shall appear spontaneously."
Having spoken these words, the Earth Deity opened the ground and presented him with a sword and a staff.
He then advanced, surrounded by the fourfold army, until he reached the kingdom of Takṣaśilā.
Upon hearing that Aśoka was coming, the people of the country naturally submitted to him.
They adorned the city grounds and leveled the roads;
each person carried a flask filled with precious substances and covered the top with flowers, calling them "auspicious flasks" (*maṅgalaghaṭa*) as a sign of submission.
Meeting him half a yojana away, he spoke these words:
"I have not rebelled against the king, nor have I rebelled against the prince;
I have only opposed the wicked ministers who stand at the king's side."
Having been honored, revered, and escorted into the city,
the people were pacified and returned to their kingdom.
The king then dispatched Aśoka to punish the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
The people of that country welcomed and accommodated him just as before, without any difference.
Once they had been pacified and brought into harmony, he returned to his own country.
There were two great wrestlers who attended upon Aśoka.
Aśoka immediately granted the two men fiefdoms.
At that time, the celestial deity protected the kingdom and proclaimed: "Be careful not to rebel!"
For what reason? Aśoka ought to become a Cakravartin King over one quarter of the world;
gradually subduing and punishing all within the four seas, they shall all submit and come under his rule.
Just as the elder brother of Aśoka, named Susīma, was entering the city of Puṣpapura,
the chief minister was about to leave the city;
they met one another on the road.
The minister’s head was bald and shorn.
Because Susīma was laughing and joking, he struck the minister on the head with his hand.
The minister thought to himself, "This prince has not yet succeeded to the throne."
He then used his power and influence to drive me from my head;
had he ascended the throne, he would surely have severed my head with a blade.
He then spoke to the five hundred ministers regarding the transgressions of Susīma, declaring that he was unfit to be king.
The physiognomists prophesied that only Aśoka was destined to become a Cakravartin King of the fourth rank.
We, your ministers, should therefore establish him together.
Later, however, the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, instigated by wicked ministers, rebelled once again.
The king immediately dispatched Susīma to go there and subdue them.
When Susīma arrived, he was unable to bring those people into submission.
King Bimbisāra heard that he had failed to subdue that country.
As soon as he fell ill, he commanded his ministers to summon Susīma to be the crown prince and ordered Aśoka to go forth to wage punitive military action.
At that time, the chief ministers devised a plan for him.
He then smeared yellow substances on Aśoka’s body,
washed him with the juice of the *rākṣasa* plant, and set him aside;
he then falsely claimed that Aśoka had contracted a disease of vomiting blood and was unfit for military service.
At that time, King Bindusāra was gravely ill,
and his remaining life was but brief.
After the minister Rūpārāma had attended to him, he addressed the king, saying:
"Please install Aśoka as king together to govern the affairs of state;
when Susīma arrives, he shall return and depose him.
Aśoka thought to himself, "If I possess the power of merit, I ought to become king."
"The deva should tie a celestial silk cloth upon my crown.
Having spoken these words, he should say, "Tie it now.
When the King saw that the deva Aśoka had tied the celestial silk cloth upon his crown, [he was satisfied].
In a state of extreme rage, blood boiled forth from his face and he passed away.
Aśoka was established as king, and Raudrākṣa was made the chief minister.
When Susīma heard that his father the king had passed away and Aśoka had been established as king,
he conceived a heart of wrath and returned to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
When Aśoka heard that Susīma was coming, [he prepared for him].
He stationed one mighty warrior at the first gate,
a second mighty warrior at the second gate,
and a third mighty warrior at the third gate.
He placed Rādhagupta beneath the eastern gate,
while Aśoka took charge of it himself,
stationing a mechanical white elephant there.
On the elephant, an image of Aśoka was painted;
around its four sides, a great fire pit was constructed and covered with dung and straw.
Susīma approached toward the third gate.
Ratigupta said to Susīma, "Aśoka is now at the eastern gate; enter through him.
If you succeed in gaining entry, he shall become your minister."
"If he cannot harm Aśoka, then even entering through this gate will be of no avail.
Thereupon, Susīma went directly to the eastern gate and proceeded straight toward the elephant, intending to seize Aśoka.
Unaware, they fell into a pit of fire and were extinguished.
At that time, there was a powerful man named Bhadrayudha among the Susīmā,
who led tens of thousands of troops into the Buddha-dharma.
When those who had left the household life attained the path of Arhatship, the various ministers and high officials began to despise Aśoka.
Aśoka secretly desired to punish them;
he immediately told the ministers to cut down fine trees bearing flowers and fruit and to surround them with thorny brambles.
The minister replied, "I have always heard that thorny hedges are used to surround groves of flowers and fruit;
I have never heard of using fine trees of flowers and fruit to surround thorns."
Even after being commanded three times, the ministers stubbornly refused to comply.
The king, overcome with extreme rage, immediately executed these five hundred great ministers.
Later, during the spring season, he went to the pleasure grove surrounded by his palace ladies.
There was a tree named Aśoka whose flowers were exceedingly lovely.
Because the Aśoka was of the same name as himself, he cherished this tree with great affection.
The body of the Aśoka, however, was coarse and rough to the touch.
Because King Aśoka’s body was coarse and rough, the various court ladies felt no affection or respect for him and took no pleasure in being near him;
they waited until he was asleep and went to play in the garden.
Upon seeing the aśoka tree, he immediately snapped off its flowering branches.
When the king awoke from his sleep and saw that the tree had been destroyed, he asked his attendants,
"Who has ruined this tree?"
He replied, "The palace women have defiled it.
The king became greatly incensed; he seized five hundred palace women, led them around the tree, and burned them to death.
All the people of the kingdom cried out that he was cruel and evil.
Consequently, he was named Aśoka the Wicked.
At that time, Rādhagupta addressed the king, saying:
"To personally commit such slaughter is not fitting for a king."
"The King should now select wicked men to punish those who have committed crimes.
The king approved these words and immediately dispatched messengers to recruit such men.
On a mountain at the frontier of the kingdom, there was a weaver.
He begot a son named Kiri, who was extremely wicked;
he reviled his father and reviled his mother,
holding a net in his hand and setting a trap with his feet.
When insects or beasts touch the leaves of this plant smeared with poison,
none fail to die instantly;
all people alike call it a great evil.
The entire kingdom designated him as Aṅguli;
they sent him to that place and said to Aṅguli,
"Are you able to punish criminals for King Aśoka?"
Jīrī replied, "If I am capable of governing even the wicked people of the world,
how much more so a single Aśoka?
How could I possibly be unable?"
The messenger was told these words and reported them in full to the king.
The king immediately summoned him.
When Gīrī heard that the messenger had come to summon him, he went.
He immediately took leave of his parents;
when they would not grant him permission, he killed them.
He then sent a messenger to ask Jīrī why he was late.
Giri replied, "My parents would not permit it;
I have delayed only because I had to kill them.
Thereupon, he accompanied the messenger to see the king and addressed him, saying:
"Construct for me a prison that is exceedingly severe, yet make it pleasant and delightful.
Once the prison is finished, name it the 'Delightful Prison' (Kāmarati).
Furthermore, report to the King: 'If anyone enters, do not permit them to leave.'"
The king immediately granted his consent.
Then that wicked Kīrī went to the Kukkuṭārāma monastery.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in that monastery.
The *Āṭānāṭiya Sūtra* states:
"Those who delight in the boiling cauldrons shall be pounded with mortars;
those who delight in mortars and pestles shall be boiled in cauldrons."
In the hells, they swallow great iron balls and have molten copper poured into their mouths.
Having heard these words, he immediately thought to himself:
"I shall also do this within my own city of hell."
At that time, there was an elder and his wife who,
taking one another as companions, entered the sea to gather treasures.
Upon reaching the middle of the ocean, they gave birth to a son.
He was immediately given the name Sāgara.
After twelve years had passed, he went out to sea;
there he encountered five hundred bandits who plundered his wealth and murdered the elder.
Thereupon, Sāgara left the household life to study the Way.
Wandering from place to place for alms, he arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra;
not recognizing the village, he entered the prison of "Delight" and spoke these words:
The exterior appearance was lovely, but the interior was like a hell.
He then wished to go out, but Jīrṇa would not permit it, saying to the bhikṣu:
"You shall now undergo the penalty of death here; how can you wish to leave?"
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu immediately wept aloud.
Kīli asked him, "Why do you weep so loudly like an infant?
The bhikṣu replied, "I do not weep out of fear of death; rather, I weep because I fear losing the opportunity for wholesome benefit."
"Why is this? I have only recently left the household life and have not yet realized the Dharma.
A human body is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha-Dharma is difficult to encounter; for this reason, I weep.
Kīli said, "O King, first please listen to me."
"Whoever enters this city shall not be permitted to leave; they must be sought out and punished.
The bhikṣu said, "Grant me seven days to live.
He was granted permission immediately upon saying, "Kill him according to your will."
At that time, King Aśoka, seeing his palace women engaged in affectionate conversation with other men,
became enraged and cast them into the prison of "Affection.
Immediately thereafter, Kīlāli began to pound them with pestles.
As the pestle struck down, his head was crushed and his eyeballs fell out.
Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu conceived a sense of revulsion and thought:
"Alas! The words of the Great Compassionate One are truly authentic."
It is said that form is precarious and fragile, like a mass of foam;
it is not solid, quickly decays, and does not remain for even a moment.
Where now is that handsome countenance?
The fine complexion and thin skin are likewise subject to decay.
How strange that birth and death are what the ignorant and foolish delight in, rather than the noble Dharma!
Seeing this realm, one should have no regrets at the time of death.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu observed throughout the night;
severing the various fetters, he attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
Thus, through such diligent effort, he eventually further attained the path of arhatship.
When the seven days had already passed, Kīli spoke, saying, "The seven days are over;
as the eighth day is about to dawn, you may undergo your punishment.
The bhikṣu replied, "My night has already passed; my day has already dawned."
"The time for your benefit has arrived; you shall be punished according to your deeds.
Kīli asked, "What do you mean by 'my night has passed, my day has dawned, and the time for my benefit has arrived'?"
"Please explain this extensively for me.
The bhikṣu replied, "In the past, during the night of darkness and ignorance,
the enemies that are the fetters have all been eternally extinguished."
This is called "my night has passed";
with wisdom and an empty mind, one clearly perceives the three realms.
This is called "the sun has risen."
"What the Buddha has intended, I have now fully accomplished.
This is what is called 'the time for benefit having arrived.
Let your old age and lifespan be treated as you wish."
Giri was evil at heart and committed cruel acts without remorse;
disbelieving in the afterlife, he gave rise to intense hatred and prepared a large cauldron, placing water within it.
It was completely filled with fat, grease, blood, marrow, excrement, urine, and all manner of foul impurities.
He then took the bhikṣu and threw him into it;
he lit a great fire beneath it, yet even when the wood and grass were nearly consumed, he could not make it hot enough.
Thereupon, Jīri became enraged and struck the one who had lit the fire with a staff;
yet his own hands were not burned even though he handled the firewood until it was entirely consumed.
Furthermore, he set ablaze the rafters of the house, along with ghee, cotton cloths, and various layers of cloth, causing them all to burn away, yet the water remained as cold as before.
Wondering at the cause of this,
he looked into the cauldron and saw the aforementioned bhikṣu sitting cross-legged upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower.
At that time, Gīrī was greatly astonished by the reason for this.
He went at once to inform the king, who immediately came to look;
he broke down a wall and entered, followed by all the people—several thousand myriads of koṭis—who watched this bhikṣu.
At that time, the bhikṣu saw that the immeasurable multitude of those ready for conversion had all assembled;
he immediately emerged from the cauldron, his robes clean and pure,
so that there was no one among the great assembly who did not behold him.
Leaping into the void, he performed various transformations;
water issued from his upper body while fire issued from his lower body,
appearing like a great mountain manifesting in mid-air.
Having seen this, the king was struck with wonder;
gazing up at him with reverence, he joined his palms in contemplation and spoke these words:
"This bhikṣu, like us, has received a human body from the same source."
"Your majestic virtue is most sublime, transcending all worldly realms.
You leap into the void and manifest great supernormal powers.
I do not yet understand this; I only pray that you will explain it well."
"I have thus come to understand your noble undertaking;
I shall practice it according to my own ability.
At that time, the bhikṣu knew that King Aśoka was a great donor who would surely be able to distribute the Buddha’s relics to benefit devas and humans.
At that time, the Buddha said: "I am the Great Compassionate One who severs the fetters.
The sons of the Buddha have already attained liberation within the three realms of existence and have been disciplined by the Tamer."
It is extinguished by those who seek quiescence;
it is liberated by those who seek liberation.
Great King, you should know that the Buddha has also prophesied for you that, one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [you shall attain this].
In the city of Pāṭaliputra, there was a king named Aśoka,
a Cakravartin who ruled over one-quarter of the world;
as a King of the True Dharma, he widely distributed the relics.
Whereas [in the past] eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas were erected,
you, O King, have now instead constructed a great prison-city resembling a hell,
where you slaughter the lives of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
"Great King, you should now grant fearlessness to all sentient beings.
You should also fulfill the intentions of the Buddhas.
O Śakra among men, you must surely bestow fearlessness and give rise to a heart of compassion."
He distributed the relics extensively to provide true salvation for all.
Upon hearing these words, the king conceived deep faith and realization within the Buddha-dharma;
with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus to the Son of the One Possessing Ten Powers:
I have previously committed transgressions of extreme gravity; please accept my repentance.
I now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the sublime Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
May you cause me to cultivate meritorious deeds that shall adorn the great earth.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately ascended into the air and departed; the king also wished to depart.
However, Agharī said, "The king previously made an agreement with me that no one who enters this prison shall be permitted to leave."
The king then spoke to him, saying, "Do you wish to kill me? He replied, "I wish to kill you.
The king said, "Did you enter first, or did I enter first?
He replied to the king, "I entered first."
The king said, "Since you entered first, you should be the first to receive punishment.
The king immediately dispatched men to seize Ghiri and place him within a house of lacquer resin, where he was burned to death with fire.
Thus, he destroyed the prison of craving and attachment, bestowing fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
He then proceeded to Rājagṛha and took the four *śīrṣa* measures of relics that King Ajātaśatru had buried.
He immediately erected a great stūpa at this very spot.
He likewise took all the relics buried in the second, third, and up to the seventh locations.
Thereupon, they proceeded again to the village of Rāma.
The Nāga King of the Sea, wishing to take some of the *śarīra* relics,
immediately came out and invited the King to enter his palace.
The king then disembarked from his boat and entered the dragon palace.
The dragon addressed the king, saying, "I only pray that you will leave these relics here to allow me to make offerings to them; please do not take them away.
When the king saw how the Dragon King paid such respectful homage and made offerings, he found it to be many times greater than those made by humans.

"Is it because of the conditions of past virtuous karma that he is named Śāṇakavāsin?

"My son, because you have manifested such joy, you shall obtain great merit.
Then, before the merchant leader, he flew into the air, performed various miraculous transformations, and entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the merchant leader was none other than myself.

"Because of my greed and stinginess in a previous life, I have now become impoverished.
Today I have no wealth with which to cultivate merit.
Thus the husband and wife deliberated together.
"We shall pledge our bodies as collateral for wealth.
Rare indeed are meritorious deeds;
would it not be a source of great joy to obtain wealth and give it away?"
The husband and wife went together immediately to a wealthy family and said,
"Give us seven gold coins;
we will pledge our bodies for seven days."
"If we do not obtain it, my body and my wife shall become your slaves.
Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with joy and immediately gave him seven coins.
Thereupon, the husband and wife took these coins and gave them to the solicitor.
The exhorter asked,
"From where did you obtain this money with which you have used for almsgiving?
The husband and wife replied:
Being destitute and utterly lacking wealth,
he rejoiced at having encountered a field of merit but had no means to cultivate it;
therefore, he borrowed this money from a wealthy householder, pledting his own body as collateral.
If the time limit has expired, it is permitted for the husband and wife to become slaves.
The one who exhorted them said:
"To pledge or borrow in such a manner is extremely difficult."
"What is the use of giving?
The poor man replied, "In my previous life I did not practice such deeds;
today, already in distress, I am suffering this poverty."
Therefore, I now exert effort in giving through hired labor.
By these causes and conditions,
I vow that my future bodies shall surely attain wealth and happiness.
When the king arrived at the palace, he took his own garments, necklaces, and the horse upon which he had ridden, along with the garments and necklaces of his various consorts,
and immediately bestowed them, together with a large village, as a fief upon that man.
King Aśoka of the city thus exhorted and transformed them;
merit and evil, being of the same nature, were immediately extinguished.
Formerly, King Aśoka wished to seize the palace occupied by King Ajātaśatru;
therefore, he cast a great iron wheel-sword into the Ganges River and caused the water-wheel to revolve.
At the place where the śarīra was enshrined, they attempted to take it by various means but were unable to do so.
They asked the bhikṣu Padma,
"How can it be obtained?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"If one were to throw several thousand hu of mangoes into it, the wheel could be brought to a halt.
He then followed these instructions.
He placed a pear into the water;
as soon as one pear happened to fall into the mechanism,
the sword-wheel within the aperture immediately stopped and no longer revolved.
However, it was entirely impossible for the Great Dragon King to provide protection.
The king then asked,
"By what means can this be achieved?"
The Dragon King’s merit is so superior that it cannot be fathomed.
He asked:
"How is it known that his merit is superior?"
He had images of a dragon and of the king cast from gold and weighed them on a scale;
whichever was heavier possessed the superior merit.
Immediately, the dragon image was weighed and found to be twice as heavy.
Upon seeing this, the king diligently cultivated merit.
Having cultivated merit, he—
They cast the image once more and weighed it again;
the weight of the King’s image and the Dragon’s image were exactly equal.
The king further cultivated merit and once again cast an image for inspection;
yet the king’s image became increasingly heavy. When the king realized the image was heavy, he understood its significance.
He led his host of troops to the edge of the water.
The Nāga King came forth in person and offered various kinds of jewels.
The King spoke to the Nāga:
King Ajātaśatru has sent me some śarīra relics,
which I now wish to take;
the Naga King knew for himself that his own power was inferior.
The King was then led to the site of the relics; he opened the door and took the relics to bestow them.
Just as the oil lamps prepared by King Ajātaśatru were about to go out, the moment the relics emerged, the lamps were completely extinguished.
The king, finding this strange, questioned the Lotus Bhikṣu:
"How is it that King Ajātaśatru measured out the oil for the lamp,
and it was only when he had taken the śarīra that it finally went out?"
The Venerable One replied:
"At that time, there was a skilled mathematician who calculated that such an amount of oil would be consumed over the course of a hundred years."
It was because of such calculations that [the matter] has continued until the present day.
